# Diagnosing Brake Light Failure on the 2002 Dodge Durango

When three of your four tail lights illuminate but the brake function fails specifically on the third unit, you are looking at a classic electrical isolation issue rather than a total system failure. The fact that the third light cluster powers up when the ignition is on and the headlights work indicates that the bulb itself, the socket wiring, and the ground connection for that specific lamp are likely intact. The problem lies in the path of current between the brake pedal switch and the bulb.

On the 2002 Dodge Durango, this behavior narrows the diagnostic scope significantly. Since the third tail light is non-functional only under braking conditions while functioning as a running light, the high-current path to that specific filament is interrupted at the source or by a faulty control component. The most probable culprit is the brake light switch located on the top of the brake pedal arm. Over time, the internal contacts within this switch can corrode or the mechanical plunger can lose its tension, failing to close the circuit when pressure is applied.

To verify this, you should inspect the brake light switch before assuming a wiring harness failure. Locate the switch mounted near the pedal pivot point and disconnect the electrical connector. Using a multimeter set to continuity mode, probe the terminals on the switch side of the connector while someone presses the brake pedal fully to the floor. If there is no continuity (no beep or zero ohms) when the pedal is depressed, the internal contacts are open. This is a common failure mode where the micro-switch inside the assembly sticks or corrodes, effectively breaking the circuit for that specific output while leaving the running light path unaffected if the circuit design uses separate pins for running and braking functions.

If the switch tests good, you must then investigate the wiring harness integrity, specifically looking for broken wires near the suspension mounts. The 2002 Durango is known for chafing wires where the body panel flexes against the undercarriage, particularly on the driver's side or rear axle areas. However, given that two other tail lights work perfectly, a complete harness failure affecting only one lane of the circuit is less likely than a localized switch issue or a blown fuse dedicated to the third brake light circuit if the vehicle uses a fused split for running and braking lights.

Check the fuse box under the hood for fuses labeled "TAIL/LIGHT" or similar, though often these systems share a common feed. If the vehicle uses a separate relay or fuse for the brake lights specifically, verify that the fuse is not blown. You can swap it with a known good fuse of identical amperage to rule out a blown internal element.

Another potential, though less common, failure point is the third tail light bulb itself. Some bulbs have dual filaments; one for running lights and one for brake lights. If the base connection for the high-intensity filament has corroded or if the glass-to-metal seal on that specific filament side has degraded, you will see the low-current running light work but fail to illuminate when the higher current of the braking circuit is applied. Inspect the bulb socket for signs of arcing or melted plastic, which would indicate a loose connection preventing high-current flow.

Finally, consider the integration with the Body Control Module (BCM). While rare on this model year without other electrical gremlins, the BCM can sometimes fail to send the ground signal to the brake lights if the input from the brake switch is interpreted incorrectly as an open circuit due to voltage spikes or internal corrosion. However, in 90% of these cases, replacing the mechanical brake light switch resolves the issue immediately. Always start with the simplest mechanical component before moving toward complex wiring diagnostics or electronic module replacements.
